idiom_name: try-with-resources over AutoCloseable (try (var r = open()) { ... }); java.lang.ref.Cleaner for lifetimes that are not one block
implementation_notes: The classic owner contract is AutoCloseable/Closeable, and the compiler-supplied destructor call is the try-with-resources statement: resources declared in the try header are closed in reverse declaration order on every exit path, and when both the body and close() fail the body's exception propagates with the close failure attached as a suppressed exception instead of being masked. The statement handles multiple resources and any effectively-final variable (Java 9+), so a wrapper class is only needed when the ownership rule must be reusable or enforced at a boundary. Resources whose lifetime is not one lexical scope use java.lang.ref.Cleaner (Java 9+), which runs a registered action when the object becomes phantom-reachable - a safety net, not a release point - because finalize() is deprecated for removal and GC timing is unpredictable.
pitfalls: try-with-resources covers only the resources named in its header: a second handle acquired inside the body (or stored in a field and a collection) is not closed by the statement and needs its own try-with-resources or an explicit finally.

A failed close is attached to the body's exception as a suppressed exception, so code that catches and logs only the primary exception loses the cleanup failure - inspect getSuppressed() wherever teardown can fail.

Cleaner is not RAII: its action runs on a cleaner thread after phantom reachability, may run long after the resource was last used, and may never run before JVM exit; never use it for pool leases, locks or anything the program keeps using.
